On anchoring bias: 

My go to source in information about a neighbourhood, apartment or a house is its neighbors. I go, knock on their doors and talk to them. You can get all sorts of information but don't ask their opinion on the price.

The neighbours are using old, unusually low home prices as their reference point. Because those prices are anchored in their memory, the current higher price feels excessive—even if the market has fundamentally changed.

Likewise, when a stock is breaking out to all-time highs, you don't ask an investor/trader who has been dealing with it all the time. They will tell you, it is pricey/overvalued at these levels. 

You are a fresh mind, patient and if you have done your homework, be optimistic.

Details, details, details. Everything is in the details. 

Small touches makes a huge difference.

To identify cyclical bull markets, we first must identify the bear markets, since the bulls fill up the space in between. Again, there is no hard and fast rule here, including the 20% drawdown threshold. Since 1950, six out of ten bear markets were recessions (growth shocks) and four out of ten were not (mostly rate shocks). We have short-but-sharp cycles like the 1987 crash, which may not be bear markets at all. The average drawdown for equities has been 30%, and the average duration has been 11 months. The average P/E compression has been 37%. 🧵(2/2)

Now that the cyclical bull is 48 months old, where to next? Is there a cookie-cutter playbook for when and how bull markets end? Unfortunately, no. Every cycle is different, and that certainly seems true today. With the caveat that identifying cycles is more an art than science, the table below shows my take on all the cyclical bull and bear markets since the 19th century. The averages at the bottom of the table are since 1950. 🧵(1/2)

To be fair, today earnings are booming not because of a base effect from the COVID recession but a historic technological breakthrough. This is pushing margins to the highest levels ever (now 17.4%), which is a far cry from where we were in 2021. Note in the chart below that valuations and margins move in lockstep. Perhaps current earnings growth is much more sustainable since there is no recession base effect this time. But “this time is different” are words that should be carefully chosen, no matter how exciting the circumstances.🧵(3/3)

The glaring exception to this rule was the 2021 liquidity bubble. Rather than paying less for peak earnings growth, investors went right over the cliff, paying 21x expected earnings (purple circles) when earnings growth was already at the right tail. I point this out because it’s notable that investors are currently paying a similar multiple (19x) for earnings that are growing 30-40%, whereas in the past they would have only been willing to pay 12x on average. 🧵(2/3)

The big question is whether the current 30-40% growth rate in earnings can be sustained, and what investors should pay for what could soon be peak earnings growth. Below we see a distribution of the 12-month trailing earnings growth rate since 1950, overlaid against the prevailing n12m P/E-multiple at each of those bins (orange circles). We appear to be on the right tail in terms of earnings growth, and the chart shows that investors have tended to not want to pay top dollar for peak earnings growth. Makes sense since earnings are generally cyclical. 🧵(1/3)

For a period of time I took care of management of passive funds. The most difficult to manage in the presence of illiquid stocks/markets. 

Stock price goes up. Its weight in the fund increases. You need to reduce and rebalance according to the weight in the benchmark. But the stock moved up on thin volume and you have large quantity to reduce. 

You can only deviate certain basis points from the benchmark.

So many indexed/passive funds out there...

Index providers add/remove stocks from the benchmarks.

Fund managers need to follow and rebalance.

A pick up in volume and transactions...

Is the volume spike meaningful data point?

Think of the same in small or mid cap stocks when funds get involved...

Is it the market or few large portfolio's decision?
